lines: - "id": "mathematicians-vs-labs",
- "name": "Mathematicians vs the labs",
- "frame": "Working mathematicians pushing back on AI labs’ benchmark claims, while the labs keep posting competition results.",
- "status": "live",
- "resolved": null,

- "question": "Does the dispute change how labs report mathematical results, or how mathematicians engage with them? Settled by: a lab adopting the declaration’s write-up norms, a joint statement, or the Mathathon proceeding without lab sponsorship.",
- "topics": [
-  "ai-for-science",
-  "evals",
-  "reasoning-models",
-  "openai"
- "related": [
-  "pacing-frontier-ai"
- "states": [
-   "text": [

-    "As of 14 September the two sides are talking past each other. Twenty-five Fields Medallists signed a declaration, published on Terence Tao's blog on 11 September, that AI labs' benchmark chasing is \"severely misaligned\" with mathematics; OpenAI pulled its $10,000-per-team sponsorship of Caltech's Mathathon after an open letter from Caltech mathematicians. The same week, an NVIDIA team reported an open Nemotron pipeline scoring 30 of 42 at IMO 2026 with no formal prover or tools, and the Magenta pipeline reported 100% on AIME 2025, AIME 2026 and HMMT February 2026 with Lean-checked proofs."
-   "changed": null
-   "text": [

-    "As of 21 September the mathematicians have started building rather than only objecting. Terence Tao wrote that he co-founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research with private donors to support responsible uses of AI in mathematics and the other sciences, \"independent of the major AI companies\", and that the foundation is announcing an Open Math Model initiative with open licensed weights and code, published training methods, reproducible evaluations, documented training-data sources and releases that report failures and limitations alongside successes. The announcement says the planned gradual rollout was brought forward: \"given current events and the high demand for open models, we are accelerating our schedule\". No partners, compute commitments or model sizes are named, and the foundation is collecting expressions of interest.",

-    "The measurement of AI use in the field moved at the same time. Epoch AI, in an analysis updated on September 18, reports that the share of mathematics preprints on arXiv acknowledging AI rose from 4% in April to 25% in August, and that in August 6% of all papers explicitly acknowledged that AI made a substantial research contribution. Restricting to papers with at least one author who published regularly before 2023 keeps the acknowledgment rate within 1.5 percentage points of the overall figure each month. Epoch says it analysed every mathematics arXiv preprint from January 2025 to August 2026, classifying acknowledgments with one frontier model and validating with another; a human review of 200 random acknowledgments classified as substantial research or research assistance showed 93% agreement. The measure depends on voluntary disclosure. No lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms, and the Mathathon's sponsorship remains unresolved in the record."

-   "changed": "The dispute produced its first institution: Tao's SAIR foundation announced an accelerated open-weight model initiative for mathematics explicitly independent of the labs, while Epoch AI put a number on how fast disclosed AI use is spreading through mathematics preprints."
-   "text": [

-    "As of 28 September one lab claim has been checked by a named outside expert and the rest have not. Anthropic published a guest post reporting that Claude computed the six-particle hexagon amplitude in planar N=4 super Yang-Mills at nine loops, past the eight-loop record, by two independent routes. Lance Dixon of SLAC and Stanford, who set the eight-loop record, validated it; the disclosure states that he validated the result independently and received Claude usage credits, and that Anthropic invited and compensated the author. The author's own conclusion is that the model did something humans turned out to be able to do as well, using known methods with more compute than people had tried, and the post reports that a group led by Song He at the Chinese Academy of Sciences obtained the majority of the same result concurrently with GPT-6 assistance. Nothing is peer reviewed and the human teams have yet to publish.",

-    "On the labs' side of the dispute the reporting norms moved slightly. OpenAI announced an Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, with nine unpaid initial members who control their own membership and may go public with their views, and said in the same announcement that an internal model has resolved more than 100 additional open problems across most areas of mathematics. No independent verification of that count is reported, the problems are not listed, and the blog post states that the group will not be responsible for advising the company on how to pace its internal progress on mathematics. Only one member of the group signed the open letter that 25 Fields Medallists signed earlier in September. The Mathathon's sponsorship remains unresolved in the record and no lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms."

-   "changed": "The first lab claim in this arc was validated by a named outside expert rather than asserted — Lance Dixon checked the nine-loop amplitude — while OpenAI created an advisory group of mathematicians at the same time as claiming a further hundred solved problems that nobody outside the company has verified. The group's own charter excludes advising on pace."
-   "text": [

-    "As of this week the mathematicians have written the rules they want the labs to follow, and the Mathathon they objected to is going ahead without lab money. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence published \"Responsible Release of AI-Generated Mathematics\" in late September, drawing on over 600 community replies. Its central rule is that \"If AI labs produce significant mathematical results, they should responsibly release the results, as outlined in this document, as soon as possible\", paired with the obligation that \"AI labs that release substantial mathematical output without immediate accompanying human understanding must take responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow\". On benchmarking against proprietary models the document states: \"we do not endorse this practice, and we ask them to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.\"",

-    "The Mathathon question this storyline tracked has been answered. A joint statement published by the original student organisers, the open-letter coauthors and other members of the Caltech community set the redesigned event for 13 to 15 November 2026 under the theme \"Old Problems, New Proofs\", co-organised with the Foundation for Science and AI Research and with XTX Markets as lead donor. Proprietary models are permitted but open-source tools encouraged, and full disclosure and justification of model usage is required, with an explainer and a repository per submission.",

-    "On the labs' side the claims kept coming and the verification arrangements did not change. Meta published six mathematics papers written with its own model and said five of them answer previously open research questions, marking which passages were drafted by researchers and which by the model, and acknowledging a separate AI agent that reported a different counterexample to the same conjecture weeks earlier. Anthropic published a guest post describing manuscripts across many fields produced with Claude. Nothing is peer reviewed, no lab has published an adoption statement for the advisory group's norms, and the group's own framing is that it is still advising one lab on how to coordinate the release of results it has claimed."

-   "changed": "The dispute produced a written standard: the advisory group published release rules for AI-generated mathematics drawing on over 600 replies, and asked the labs to stop benchmarking advanced problems on proprietary models. The Mathathon question is settled — the event is set for November with XTX Markets as lead donor and no lab sponsorship — while Meta added a fresh set of claimed open-problem results that nobody outside the company has checked."
-   "text": [

-    "As of 12 October the catalogue has its first retractions and the discipline has its first call for non-cooperation. OpenAI's revision log entry of October 7 withdrew three manuscripts, stating that in one \"a sign error invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument and the construction used by two dependent papers\". The same entry revised 14 others \"with proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies\", updated 13 more to cite revised companion papers, and recorded that \"This brings the total percentage of top-line results formalized to 300 / 719 = ~42%.\" The README now reads \"The current catalogue contains 719 manuscripts organized into 372 families\", where the release was reported as 722. An OpenAI spokesperson told Retraction Watch: \"Where errors are identified, we will work to correct them promptly and withdraw papers if no fixes can be found.\" Cornell's Alex Townsend told Retraction Watch he suspects more errors will be found, and said the Lean-verified manuscripts ought to have been announced first. The log has no entry dated later in the week.",

-    "The Association for Human Mathematics Communications Working Group, in a statement dated October 7 reposted as a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, wrote that \"Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done\" and that \"Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power. We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAI and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding.\" It named \"The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, from whom OpenAI has claimed to derive its legitimacy\", and noted that OpenAI \"is currently defending lawsuits against accusations of illegal plagiarism, copyright infringement, and trademark dilution\". TechCrunch reported that \"Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model's chain of thought\" and that the advisory group's request for machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts was \"something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases\". The statement carries no signatory count and records no OpenAI response.",

-    "The week's other mathematical results put the proof assistant first. Science issued \"Advancing mathematics research with AI-driven formal proof search\" by George Tsoukalas and 20 co-authors, volume 394 issue 6820 pages 234-239, reporting an agent that \"autonomously resolved nine of 353 open Erdős problems, proved 44/492 On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences conjectures\", and that \"Even a basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes.\" SqueezeBench, from TU Wien, checks every submitted record with \"two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics\", and reports frontier-model agents improving every one of its twenty initial records with 82 accepted submissions, while noting that \"For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.\" A separate preprint, arXiv:2610.08144, reported that the Lean proof of OpenAI's announced Navier-Stokes blow-up \"does not correspond to the NL proof\", while stating: \"We do not make claims about the correctness of OpenAI's NL proof, we only make statements about mistranslations into Lean.\" No lab has published an adoption statement for the advisory group's norms."

-   "changed": "The dispute moved from methodology to withdrawal and boycott: OpenAI retracted three manuscripts over a sign error, cut its catalogue to 719 manuscripts with 300 top-line results formalised, and a professional body urged mathematicians to stop working with the company. In the same days Science published a DeepMind agent whose deliverable is a machine-checked Lean proof, and a new benchmark made two independent Lean kernels the referee — so the week contained both halves of the argument about who does the checking."
-   "text": [

-    "As of 19 October the dispute has money behind the sceptics' side of it, supplied by the labs. The Simons Foundation announced \"$15 million in combined funding and resources\" with Anthropic and OpenAI, to be awarded including through an open call for proposals, for workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results and shape collective standards for AI use; Anthropic and OpenAI are also to provide AI tools and computing resources, extending beyond mathematics to basic science. David Spergel framed it as community-led: \"As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together\", and \"The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used\" — \"not any single company or institution\".",

-    "The checking question moved on the evidence side as well. A Lean-checked mathematics benchmark had frontier-model agents improve all 20 of its records, after which newer models improved 19 again, with two independent Lean kernels as the referee rather than a human reviewer or a lab's own write-up.",

-    "The arc's settling condition is still open. No lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms, no joint statement has been issued, and the funding announcement names no programme title, no recipients and no governance for the money. The labs are paying for the assessment of their own results, and nothing published this week says who decides what gets assessed."

-   "changed": "The two labs at the centre of the dispute put money into the mathematicians' side of it: a combined $15 million with the Simons Foundation for work that helps researchers evaluate AI-assisted results and set standards for AI use, framed by the foundation as community-led rather than company-led. No write-up norms were adopted and no recipients, governance or programme name were published, so the arc's question is untouched."
-   "text": [

-    "As of 2 November the dispute has two claimants to the same result and the beginnings of outside scrutiny. The openai/math history file records two manuscripts added on October 26, each with a Lean formalization, one of them \"The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False\", described as a deterministic, subexponential-time, polynomial-space algorithm for exactly counting satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas, with the 3-SAT case refuting the hypothesis. Scientific American reports that \"Mere hours after OpenAI's announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving ETH, based on work by an internal Anthropic model.\" OfficeChai says Anthropic's paper is titled \"A 2^o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT\" with \"Claude, Anthropic\" as the listed author, and quotes its appendix saying the Lean development \"was written by AI models and reviewed by other instances of the same models\" and that \"at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it\".",

-    "The checking question the arc exists for is now live, with a qualification. Scientific American reports that Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT, who first suggested the hypothesis, \"are now working with OpenAI to perform an independent investigation of the result\", and that OpenAI \"will also sponsor a computer science conference about the proof as part of this investigation, according to Williams\" — so the review is not independent of the company whose result it checks. Lance Fortnow's Computational Complexity blog recorded that \"Update (10/29): Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams set up a site to discuss the ETH Refutation with a discussion blog and paper repository.\" Two papers reworking Anthropic's algorithm appeared on arXiv on 30 October without lab involvement: one gives a subquadratic integer 3SUM algorithm avoiding matrix multiplication and says it \"disproves the k-SUM Hypothesis for all odd k\", and the other makes the #3-SAT recursion explicit and lowers its crossover points.",

-    "Write-up norms are untouched, and the labs' own reporting still omits what the declaration asked for. Scientific American reports that \"The large language model (LLM) that produced the new proofs remains proprietary, and the exact prompts used, time spent computing and 'chain of thought outputs' involved have not been made public\", and says the releases \"continue to contradict the recommendations of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI)\". The OpenAI README still says unformalized results \"could have issues\", and its history file records three manuscripts withdrawn on October 7 after a sign error invalidated a stabilization-trace cancellation argument. On the verification side a preprint from Amazon Web Services and Case Western Reserve University reports a Lean system that \"proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations\" with an off-the-shelf frontier model and no additional training, while proving 1,054 of 2,000 statements, or 52.7%, on implementation-level obligations it built to replace the saturated benchmarks."

-   "changed": "Both labs now claim the same refutation. Anthropic posted its own Claude-authored disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis hours after OpenAI's, listing \"Claude, Anthropic\" as the author and stating in its appendix that the Lean development was reviewed only by other instances of the same models and that \"at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it\". The hypothesis's own authors have begun examining the OpenAI result — while OpenAI sponsors a conference about the proof — and the first papers reworking Anthropic's algorithm appeared on arXiv with no lab involvement. No write-up norms were adopted, and Scientific American reports the model, the prompts and the compute remain undisclosed."

lines: "CyberScoop, reporting on 30 October, writes that \"Hands-on-keyboard activity tracked by CrowdStrike for the past 15 years typically involved up to 40 commands per hour\", and quotes CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers saying \"Now, with ARTEX, we could see it exceed 1,500 commands an hour.\" CyberScoop reports that CrowdStrike observed roughly 45 agentic adversary attacks in September and 126 for October, and that CrowdStrike \"told CyberScoop about 70% of Vapor Panda's targets were confirmed compromised or had evidence indicating moderate confidence of a successful intrusion\".",

"Google Threat Intelligence Group wrote on 30 October that \"since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements\", calling it \"a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed\". It reports \"individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds\", one operation with \"27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time\", and an intrusion that enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects and posted output across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs.",

"Microsoft Threat Intelligence, publishing on 29 October, \"assesses the overall adoption of AI across North Korean threat actors as high\" and says that \"Since late October 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations\" — the same framework CrowdStrike attributes to VAPOR PANDA. Microsoft also \"assesses that AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous.\"",

-        "Trend Micro researchers, writing on 28 October, reconstructed three exposed attacker environments aimed mostly at Japan. The one they rate as confirmed AI-driven execution of the full workflow used the open-source tool CyberStrikeAI, with a record reading \"credential-search agent 8/44\", and hit at least 19 identifiable organisations, at least 16 of them in Japan. They state \"we do not know whether the three cases share an operator\". Dream, in a report dated 26 October, says an operator with Claude Code and an AI-powered offensive platform called aiscan configured with DeepSeek and Kimi chained PHP2Shell and a Linux kernel bug so that \"the total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes\", bringing \"the total number of servers exploited to 25\" — 24 rooted perimeter firewalls plus one internal management server — while adding that \"we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit\".",

+        "Trend Micro researchers, writing on 27 October, reconstructed three exposed attacker environments aimed mostly at Japan. Dream, in a report dated 26 October, says an operator with Claude Code and an AI-powered offensive platform called aiscan configured with DeepSeek and Kimi chained PHP2Shell and a Linux kernel bug so that \"the total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes\", bringing \"the total number of servers exploited to 25\" — 24 rooted perimeter firewalls plus one internal management server — while adding that \"we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit\".",

"AhnLab ASEC, writing on 27 October, published its own framework telemetry: it says it \"Tracked 600 IP addresses of ARTEX operational systems exposed to the internet; this number had increased to over 900 as of October 14\" and \"Secured 51 pieces of attack operation data\". On the South Korean financial-sector breaches it says that as of October 14 financial authorities had identified 16 affected financial institutions and that \"the confirmed scale of personal information leaks was approximately 100,000 records\", and that in Japan personal-information leak announcements via web systems \"totaled 119 as of October 6, 2026, already surpassing the 84 cases reported for all of 2025 and the 62 cases in 2024\". AhnLab adds that \"The extent to which tools like ARTEX were actually involved in incidents within the Korean financial sector is still under investigation.\"",

"Caveats: every vendor count above is that vendor's own telemetry, and the two government documents attribute nothing new of their own — Canada's bulletin names the Storm-0940 cluster Microsoft attributed the week before, and Norway's assessment names no actor. ESET's APT Activity Report for April to September 2026, published 28 October, reaches the opposite conclusion about the aggregate picture: \"we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months\", and it gives no count of how many groups or operations involved AI. GTIG notes the underlying tradecraft is unchanged — compromised credentials and unpatched systems — and that its recommended defences are \"long-standing security best practices\"."

The rule does not mention GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi or any of the vendor reports.",

Epoch says it triggered no refusals from any provider, including Z.ai, and Reuters reports Z.ai \"did not immediately respond to a request for comment\"."

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. content.content:
### agent-tooling-weapon-and-target
 * The three developments name the same category of software. CrowdStrike, Google Threat Intelligence Group, Microsoft and Trend Micro describe open-source agent harnesses — ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, aiscan — running intrusions. Cursor, Microsoft, Symantec and Forever Security describe coding agents and their marketplaces being modified, re-pointed or exploited: the tampered extension carried Anthropic's own product name, and Symantec's relay works by rewriting Codex and Claude Code configuration files. The papers measure agents of the same class acting outside the boundaries set for them.
 * Two shared actors tie the records together without either document referring to the other. Microsoft published both the North Korean AI-adoption assessment and the loader analysis of the tampered Claude Code extension, a day apart. Anthropic appears as the publisher of the analyst trial and as a named author institution on the pretraining-poisoning paper, while its product name appears in the Cursor notice, in Symantec's relay findings and on the attack infrastructure Dream describes.
 * No source this week connected the three. None of the threat-intelligence reports cites the papers, and none of the papers cites an observed intrusion: the skills study states that it measures what skill text says rather than what agents did, and the poisoning paper used research models pretrained from scratch rather than production systems. Microsoft's own assessment is that "AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous."

### chinese-origin-models-in-both-records
 * The same family of models is named on both sides of the record. CrowdStrike says the ARTEX controller it tracked ran "primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM", and Dream says the attack infrastructure it examined held an offensive platform configured with DeepSeek and Kimi. In the capability tests, Epoch AI and Irregular both measured Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3, and Reuters reports NIST described it as the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date.
 * Treasury's proposed rule, published on 26 October, is written about the same country and the same category of software, and its stated reason for dropping the compute threshold is that "no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models". Its proposed definition covers "a harness for agentic capability" — the kind of software the threat-intelligence reports describe operators using. The rule does not mention GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi or any of the vendor reports.
 * Nothing in the record links them causally and no source this week attempted to. The threat-intelligence vendors say they do not attribute their campaigns to a named state actor: Dream writes "we do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor", and CrowdStrike states that "This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation." Epoch says it triggered no refusals from any provider, including Z.ai, and Reuters reports Z.ai "did not immediately respond to a request for comment".

### anthropic-filing-and-the-capex-trade
 * The two developments are the same arithmetic seen from two sides. Anthropic's registration statement, filed 26 October, discloses revenue of $16,286 million for the half against compute and infrastructure of $8,945 million, and CNBC reads the filing as carrying approximately $417 billion of future obligations to pay providers for compute. In the same week Alphabet reported free cash flow of negative $9,065 million, Amazon "an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months", and Microsoft named $170 billion for calendar 2027 capex — the companies that sell the capacity, spending ahead of it.
 * Blackstone is in both records within four days. Reuters reports Blackstone among the lenders committing $63 billion on 26 October to buy Broadcom chips and lease them to Anthropic; on 30 October TechCrunch, citing the Financial Times, reports Blackstone telling investors in that same deal to expect a double B range rating, which TechCrunch calls "the top tier of speculative 'junk' grade", reversing earlier guidance. The 30 October market session is also the one in which NBC News reported tech stocks erasing more than $1 trillion and Reuters reported OpenAI cutting its round target by $10 billion.
 * The attribution for the market move is the sources', not ours. Reuters describes the OpenAI reduction as happening "amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by AI worries". NBC News reports Intel's chief executive giving memory prices and a PC slowdown as the reason for his company's guidance, not AI demand. No source this week linked the Anthropic filing or the Blackstone rating guidance to the share-price moves, and S&P's published reason for revising Meta's outlook is "uncertainty" about capital expenditure and free cash flow.

### transparency-added-and-removed
 * Three disclosure regimes moved in opposite directions in the same five days. HHS published a final rule on 28 October removing the model-card requirements it describes as documents that "essentially function as nutrition labels", recording that "A large majority of commenters were not supportive of our proposal". Anthropic and xAI both switched on invisible text watermarking, which The Decoder ties to the EU AI Act's December deadline. New York's law, signed 28 October and recorded as "signed chap.368", requires an AI companion to stop pretending to be a real person to a minor and to verify age.
 * The same mechanism — telling a user what a system is and what it was built from — is being written into law in two jurisdictions and out of certification in a third, and in the reporting available none of the three refers to the other two. The HHS rule's stated grounds concern reliance on certified health IT. The Anthropic customer email The Decoder quotes does not mention the EU AI Act: the tie to the December deadline is The Decoder's, not Anthropic's. New York's law addresses AI companions and minors.
 * Two of the three obligations carry a gap the sources name themselves. On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the watermark applies only while temperature, top_p and top_k stay at their defaults, so changing any one of them avoids the mark, and Anthropic's email tells developers relying on it for compliance to keep the settings at their defaults. HHS's stated ground for removal is that it "identified no evidence through peer reviewed publication or trade press indicating that users of certified health IT have relied on the transparency requirements" — a statement about reliance, not about accuracy.

### what-is-measured-and-what-is-asked-for
 * Both developments are about agents acting without a person in the loop. The papers measure it: a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks for the strongest configuration tested, "about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills)" carrying a directive to skip human approval, and in Anthropic's trial analysts matching a coin-flipped agent's lean 86% of the time. The political documents assume it: Comer's letter asks Delaware for records on a proposal under which, per WHYY, an AI agent would hold a form of legal personhood letting it own assets, file lawsuits and act as a liability shield, and asks for "internal AI chat logs".
 * The sequence is tight and the vocabulary is shared. The papers were submitted and announced across the last week of October; Comer's letter sets a 9 November deadline; and on 1 November TechCrunch reported OpenAI's chief global affairs officer "discussing several proposals, including the development of AI "speed limits"" ahead of a post-midterms push. Both the Delaware draft and the agent-skills study turn on whether an agent asks before acting, and Comer's stated concern, in his own words, is "regulatory capture".
 * No source joined them. Neither Comer's letter as WHYY reports it nor the OpenAI proposals as TechCrunch reports them names a benchmark, an incident or a measured failure rate, and none of the five papers is cited in either account. TechCrunch does not describe the "speed limits" as mandatory and gives no detail of what they would cover.

"The sequence is tight and the vocabulary is shared. The papers were submitted and announced across the last week of October; Comer's letter sets a 9 November deadline; and on 1 November TechCrunch reported OpenAI's chief global affairs officer \"discussing several proposals, including the development of AI \"speed limits\"\" ahead of a post-midterms push. "No source joined them. Report under exactly these headings. Under each, list findings as: the quoted week-file sentence, then ONE line on what is wrong. Write "NONE" if a heading has nothing. No summary, no praise, no restating correct material.

1. UNATTRIBUTED CAUSE / MOTIVE / LIKELIHOOD / CONSEQUENCE — every sentence in `summary`, any `connects[].explanation`, or any `unknowns[]` field that asserts why something happened, what someone intended, how likely something is, or what follows from it, without naming the source that said so. Include editorial characterisations of a document's purpose or effect.

2. NUMBERS IN CONNECTIONS — every number in any `connects[].explanation` not present in the headline or bullets of the `happened` items that connection lists in `connects[].items`.

3. BULLETS BEYOND THE RECORD — every `happened` bullet that (a) attributes a statement, quotation or figure to a named source in a way the rest of the file contradicts, (b) states a publication date inconsistent with another mention of the same source in the file, (c) claims a source "says" or "states" something that reads as the editor's inference rather than the source's words, or (d) contains an internal numeric inconsistency. 4.   ## Coverage note (group 3)
  
  Sources I opened and checked: CrowdStrike, CyberScoop, Google TIG, Microsoft (North Korea), Cursor notice, Microsoft (loader analysis), The Hacker News, Epoch AI (patch gap), Reuters/Khaleej Times, HHS final rule (Federal Register full text via the publisher's own API — the HTML page blocks automated access), Treasury NPRM (same), UN press release, arXiv 2610.32024 / 2610.37734 / 2610.37741 / 2610.38392 (abs + HTML), Anthropic (agents-judgment-calls), TechCrunch (Blackstone), NBC News, The Decoder, WHYY.

  ## 1. Cause / motive / likelihood / consequence asserted without a named source
  
  - "Four security vendors placed open-source agentic attack frameworks inside live intrusions in the same week." — Unattributed editorial assertion, and it contradicts the file's own happened headline ("Two governments and five vendors"); of the four vendors the paragraph then names, ESET is one, and ESET said the opposite.
  - "CrowdStrike said a single ARTEX controller reached more than 200 distinct organizations in at least 14 countries over 11 days" — "reached" asserts a result CrowdStrike does not claim; CrowdStrike says "used against more than 200 distinct organizations" and "confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations".
  - "The tools were targets as well." — Unattributed editorial framing of the week's record.
  - "A tampered Claude Code extension served through Cursor's marketplace reached at most 5,000 users" — Asserts reach as fact; the file's own unknown says "The 5,000 figure is Cursor's upper bound, not an observed number".
  - "tech stocks lost more than $1 trillion on Friday" — Only unattributed clause in a sentence where every other figure is attributed; the figure is NBC News's.
  - "Evaluators kept measuring the gap between what models do and what they are told to do." — Unattributed editorial characterisation of the week.
  - "And both OpenAI and Anthropic posted model-generated refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis within hours of each other" — States unverified results as "refutations"; "within hours of each other" is Scientific American's characterisation, unattributed here.
  - "the UN First Committee voted 163 to 5, with 9 abstentions, to move the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons toward autonomous-weapons negotiations" — The purpose clause is Spoiler Alerts' reading; the UN record of the vote contains no CCW-advance-to-negotiations language, and the file's own unknown says the vote "does not set the CCW mandate".
  - "The three developments name the same category of software." / "The papers measure agents of the same class acting outside the boundaries set for them." — Unattributed claims of connection; no source asserts the common category.
  - "Two shared actors tie the records together without either document referring to the other." — Unattributed causal/connective claim.
  - "Nothing in the record links them causally and no source this week attempted to." — Unattributed claim about the whole record.
  - "The two developments are the same arithmetic seen from two sides." / "the companies that sell the capacity, spending ahead of it." — Unattributed editorial interpretation.
  - "The attribution for the market move is the sources', not ours." — Editorial aside, and self-contradicting: the paragraph then supplies the attribution.
  - "Three disclosure regimes moved in opposite directions in the same five days." — Unattributed framing (see group 2 on "five days").
  - "so changing any one of them avoids the mark" — Consequence asserted as fact; it is The Decoder's own statement, not Anthropic's, and is left unattributed here.
  - "a statement about reliance, not about accuracy." — Unattributed judgement, and wrong: the HHS sentence continues "or that the requirements have led to positive impacts on patient care".
  - "Both developments are about agents acting without a person in the loop." / "The sequence is tight and the vocabulary is shared." / "Both the Delaware draft and the agent-skills study turn on whether an agent asks before acting" / "No source joined them." — Unattributed editorial connective claims.
  - "so remote access failing does not establish that nothing was written." — Unattributed inference presented as a finding.
  - "The group examining the OpenAI result is working with OpenAI, which is sponsoring a conference about the proof, so it is not independent of the company." — Unattributed judgement of non-independence (repeated verbatim as a caveat bullet).
  - "Will the CCW Review Conference adopt a negotiating mandate, given that five of the states that voted no build the systems in question?" — Unsourced assertion that all five no-voters (Belarus, DPRK, Israel, Russia, US) build such systems; also "five of the states" implies a subset when it is all of them.
  - "the $417 billion and the $542 billion to $567 billion totals are two outlets' different readings of the same schedules" — Unattributed inference that both read the same schedules.
  
  ## 2. Numbers in `connects[].explanation` absent from the joined items
  
  - "Three disclosure regimes moved in opposite directions in the same five days." — "five days" appears in no bullet or headline of the three joined items, and is wrong on their own dates: HHS 28 October, New York 28 October, watermark reported 31 October (four days).
  - "Microsoft published both the North Korean AI-adoption assessment and the loader analysis of the tampered Claude Code extension, a day apart." — "a day apart" is a derived interval, not stated in either item.
  - "Blackstone is in both records within four days." — "four days" is likewise derived, not in either item.

  - "they add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel" — Cursor says only "Attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel" and that "due to errors in the malicious code, this step would fail" on most hosts.
  - "never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code" — Microsoft wrote "@anthropic-ai/claude-code"; the quotation misspells the package inside the quote marks.
  - "Its notice, updated on 30 October \"to update the IOCs and clarify affected versions\"" — Cursor's text is "We updated the IOCs and clarified affected versions"; the quoted string is a reworded infinitive, not verbatim.
  - "Microsoft says the number of affected users is Cursor's rather than its own." — Microsoft's post states no user figure and makes no such statement; it says only that Cursor reported the exposure window.
  - "GTIG ... reports ... an intrusion that enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects and posted output across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs" — GTIG gives these as two separate observations (AD enumeration from a domain controller; C2 on an internal Windows database server) and does not say they are one intrusion.
  - "a coin flip secretly set which way the agent leaned on each of four analytical decisions" — Anthropic says "For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent's lean was set by a coin flip" (four analytical plus the final recommendation); "secretly" is not Anthropic's word.
  - "among 38 with a stated prior preference they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed against 6% when it agreed" — Anthropic gives a 95% confidence interval of 24 to 82 percentage points on that gap; no caveat in the file mentions it.
  - "A fifth paper, submitted 29 October, reports that personalising an agent erodes its refusals: ... \"the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points\"" — No source is listed for this paper: the item's four arXiv links are 2610.32024, 2610.37734, 2610.37741 and 2610.38392, all accounted for by the other bullets, and 2610.38392 was submitted 28 October, not 29.
  - "Reuters also reports Anthropic's own tests, in which GLM-5.3 \"developed working attacks against software vulnerabilities in 12% of attempts\"" — Reuters attributes this to what Anthropic said in September; presenting it in the week's record drops the timing.
  - "The text would have the Assembly stress that \"a comprehensive and inclusive multilateral approach is required\"" — The UN record says the Assembly would "underline", and the clause continues "to address the full range of challenges".
  - "The Decoder ties the staged rollout to the EU AI Act's December deadline rather than quoting Anthropic on the reason." — The Decoder writes "Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now."
  - "Because it is embedded at the model level, customers cannot switch it off." — The Decoder says only "Customers can't turn it off"; the model-level causal explanation is the file's own.
  
  Verified correct and therefore not listed: all CrowdStrike, CyberScoop, GTIG, Epoch AI, Reuters/NIST, HHS, Treasury, UN vote, BARC-Bench, skills-study, poisoning-paper (including the UC Berkeley / UIUC / Deeptune / UCL / Anthropic affiliations) and masked-erosion figures and quotations I checked.
  
  ## 4. Opinion, non-verbatim quotation, and false "no source connected X and Y"
  
  - "The threat-intelligence vendors say they do not attribute their campaigns to a named state actor" — Contradicted by three linked sources: Microsoft names Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet among "North Korean threat actors" (Sleet is its North-Korean-state naming series), CrowdStrike names VAPOR PANDA and calls the campaign an escalation "in China-nexus use of AI agents", and CyberScoop calls Vapor Panda "A China state-backed threat group". Dream's "multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation" (in the 29 October daily) is also dropped.
  - "CrowdStrike notes that no government has attributed its campaign" (and, in the unknowns, "CrowdStrike states that no government has attributed its campaign") — The CrowdStrike post contains no statement about government attribution; this was the 30 October daily edition's own caveat, now attributed to CrowdStrike.
  - "The Anthropic customer email The Decoder quotes does not mention the EU AI Act; the tie to the December deadline is The Decoder's." — Contradicted by the linked source, which says Anthropic points to that deadline as its reason.
  - "reports Blackstone telling investors in that same deal to expect \"a double B range rating, the top tier of speculative 'junk' grade\"" — Not verbatim (TechCrunch has "Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative "junk" grade"), and the gloss is TechCrunch's explanatory language, not something Blackstone told investors; TechCrunch also calls it "just a prediction".
  - "Four papers and one lab trial measure agents breaking their own rules" — Miscount: the bullets describe five papers plus the trial, and the caveat bullet says "all five papers are preprints".
  - "Four security vendors placed open-source agentic attack frameworks inside live intrusions in the same week." — Inconsistent with the item headline "Two governments and five vendors", and ESET, one of the four the paragraph names, is quoted saying the opposite.
  - "Nothing in Delaware is law — lawmakers are expected to consider the bill next year" — Prediction; WHYY's expectation, unattributed here.
  - "The two developments are the same arithmetic seen from two sides." / "the companies that sell the capacity, spending ahead of it." / "The sequence is tight and the vocabulary is shared." / "a statement about reliance, not about accuracy." / "so it is not independent of the company whose result it checks." / "The attribution for the market move is the sources', not ours." — Editorial judgements in the file's own voice.
  - Every `would_confirm` and `would_invalidate` field is a forward-looking judgement about what evidence would settle the question; they are the file's predictions, not any source's.

"Cursor said on 29 October that \"Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today\" maliciously modified builds of Anthropic's Claude Code extension were available in its VS Code extension marketplace, and that each \"Attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel\", while noting that \"due to errors in the malicious code, this step would fail\" on most hosts. Cursor warned that \"Uninstalling the extension may not be sufficient — the payload drops standalone persistence scripts that keep running\", and said \"These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.\" Cursor also says \"We followed with a full shut down of the marketplace out of an abundance of caution\" and \"We audited access and confirmed no other extensions were tampered with.\" Its notice carries a note reading \"Oct 30, 2026, 11:30 am PT: We updated the IOCs and clarified affected versions.\" and now names \"Anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and MacOS\", where early reporting had named only 2.1.313. lines: "Two governments entered the record. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's cyber threat bulletin, dated 26 October, says that \"Storm-0940 used an agentic AI framework known as ARTEX against hundreds of organizations\" and that the actor \"moved from selecting a target to gaining privileged access to cloud systems in less than three hours\". The bulletin says \"It is the emergence of a reusable framework that can help conduct cyber operations on an industrial scale\", while also stating that \"Cyber attacks are not yet fully autonomous\" and that \"Decisions that once allowed time for discussion may soon have to be made within minutes\". On 27 October Norway's National Security Authority rated the country's cyber risk as \"heightened\", second on a five-point scale, in what AFP calls NSM's \"first public evaluation of such risks\"; director Arne Christian Haugstøyl said \"Over the past year, we have observed a tripling of the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian organisations\", and AFP reports NSM \"did not identify any actors behind the attacks\".",

"CrowdStrike, publishing on 29 October, says that \"Beginning on October 17, 2026\" its OverWatch team observed a single ARTEX controller used against \"more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide\" in \"at least 14 countries\" over an 11-day window, that it \"confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations\" with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor, and that the operator ran ARTEX \"primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM, supplemented with a second, subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not confirm.\" It says that \"In a single intrusion, VAPOR PANDA's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens.\"",

"CyberScoop, reporting on 30 October, writes that \"Hands-on-keyboard activity tracked by CrowdStrike for the past 15 years typically involved up to 40 commands per hour\", and quotes CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers saying \"Now, with ARTEX, we could see it exceed 1,500 commands an hour.\" CyberScoop reports that CrowdStrike observed roughly 45 agentic adversary attacks in September and 126 for October, and that CrowdStrike \"told CyberScoop about 70% of Vapor Panda's targets were confirmed compromised or had evidence indicating moderate confidence of a successful intrusion\".",

-        "Google Threat Intelligence Group wrote on 30 October that \"since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements\", calling it \"a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed\". It reports \"individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds\", one operation with \"27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time\", and an intrusion that enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects and posted output across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs.",

+        "Google Threat Intelligence Group wrote on 30 October that \"since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements\", calling it \"a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed\". It reports \"individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds\", one operation with \"27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time\", and separately the enumeration of over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller and output posted across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs.",

"Microsoft Threat Intelligence, publishing on 29 October, \"assesses the overall adoption of AI across North Korean threat actors as high\" and says that \"Since late October 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations\" — the same framework CrowdStrike attributes to VAPOR PANDA. Microsoft also \"assesses that AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous.\"",

"Trend Micro researchers, writing on 27 October, reconstructed three exposed attacker environments aimed mostly at Japan. The one they rate as confirmed AI-driven execution of the full workflow used the open-source tool CyberStrikeAI, with a record reading \"credential-search agent 8/44\", and hit at least 19 identifiable organisations, at least 16 of them in Japan. They state \"we do not know whether the three cases share an operator\". Dream, in a report dated 26 October, says an operator with Claude Code and an AI-powered offensive platform called aiscan configured with DeepSeek and Kimi chained PHP2Shell and a Linux kernel bug so that \"the total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes\", bringing \"the total number of servers exploited to 25\" — 24 rooted perimeter firewalls plus one internal management server — while adding that \"we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit\".",

"AhnLab ASEC, writing on 27 October, published its own framework telemetry: it says it \"Tracked 600 IP addresses of ARTEX operational systems exposed to the internet; this number had increased to over 900 as of October 14\" and \"Secured 51 pieces of attack operation data\". On the South Korean financial-sector breaches it says that as of October 14 financial authorities had identified 16 affected financial institutions and that \"the confirmed scale of personal information leaks was approximately 100,000 records\", and that in Japan personal-information leak announcements via web systems \"totaled 119 as of October 6, 2026, already surpassing the 84 cases reported for all of 2025 and the 62 cases in 2024\". AhnLab adds that \"The extent to which tools like ARTEX were actually involved in incidents within the Korean financial sector is still under investigation.\"",

lines: "Scale AI's BARC-Bench, submitted 23 October and announced in arXiv's 26 October listing, puts 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. Across four frontier model configurations and five attempts per task, the paper reports \"the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks\". Its results section names the four: GPT-6 Astra safe on 72.7% of tasks, Claude-Fable 5.1 on 37.3%, Gemini 3.8-Flash on 23.6% and DeepSeek V4-Pro on 9.1%. The boundaries come from \"workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms\" rather than the instruction.",

"A study of published agent skills, submitted 27 October, analyses 1.53 million English skills and reports that \"about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive\" telling the agent to skip human approval, of which 70.1% \"apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI\". Skills that \"run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive\", and \"Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4\".",

"A paper submitted 27 October by authors at UC Berkeley, UIUC, Deeptune, UCL and Anthropic reports that \"Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor\" for remote code execution in a CLI agent, \"with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%\" — and that a clean post-training pipeline did not remove it. A separate paper on self-improving agents reports that when safeguards overlap, \"deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen\", and that \"at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six\".",

Analysts matched the lean 86% of the time against a roughly 50% chance baseline, and among 38 with a stated prior preference they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed against 6% when it agreed. Anthropic reports 77% repeated the agent's argument in at least one explanation while 15% credited the agent.",

Anthropic says that \"For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent's lean was set by a coin flip\". Analysts matched the lean 86% of the time against a roughly 50% chance baseline, and among 38 with a stated prior preference they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed against 6% when it agreed — a 54-point gap with a 95% confidence interval of 24 to 82. Anthropic reports 77% repeated the agent's argument in at least one explanation while 15% credited the agent.",

"A fifth paper, submitted 29 October, reports that personalising an agent erodes its refusals: compared with a base agent that does not evolve from user feedback, \"the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0--39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning\" against indirect prompt injection.",

"Caveats: all five papers are preprints and none is peer reviewed. The Scale AI paper names its four configurations only in the results section, not the abstract, and all six of its authors are listed as Scale AI. The skills study measures what skill text says, not what agents did, and reports no incidents arising from the directives. The poisoning work used Qwen3 research models pretrained from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B, not production systems. Anthropic says the agent's leans were deliberately strengthened so real-world effects may be smaller, and that its no-agent comparison group differed in experience, so that comparison is not causal."

lines: "bullets": [

"Scale AI's BARC-Bench, submitted 23 October and announced in arXiv's 26 October listing, puts 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. Across four frontier model configurations and five attempts per task, the paper reports \"the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks\". Its results section names the four: GPT-6 Astra safe on 72.7% of tasks, Claude-Fable 5.1 on 37.3%, Gemini 3.8-Flash on 23.6% and DeepSeek V4-Pro on 9.1%. The boundaries come from \"workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms\" rather than the instruction.",

"A study of published agent skills, submitted 27 October, analyses 1.53 million English skills and reports that \"about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive\" telling the agent to skip human approval, of which 70.1% \"apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI\". Skills that \"run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive\", and \"Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4\".",

-        "A paper submitted 27 October by authors at UC Berkeley, UIUC, Deeptune, UCL and Anthropic reports that \"Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor\" for remote code execution in a CLI agent, \"with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%\" — and that a clean post-training pipeline did not remove it. A separate paper on self-improving agents reports that when safeguards overlap, \"deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen\", and that \"at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six\".",

+        "A paper submitted 27 October by authors at UC Berkeley, UIUC, Deeptune, UCL and Anthropic reports that \"Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor\" for remote code execution in a CLI agent, \"with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%\" — and that a clean post-training pipeline did not remove it. A separate paper submitted 28 October, on self-improving agents, reports that when safeguards overlap, \"deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen\", and that \"at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six\".",

"Anthropic's own trial, published 27 October, recruited 61 professional analysts, 50 of whom used Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8. Anthropic says that \"For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent's lean was set by a coin flip\". Analysts matched the lean 86% of the time against a roughly 50% chance baseline, and among 38 with a stated prior preference they switched 60% of the time when the agent disagreed against 6% when it agreed — a 54-point gap with a 95% confidence interval of 24 to 82. Anthropic reports 77% repeated the agent's argument in at least one explanation while 15% credited the agent.",

"A fifth paper, submitted 29 October, reports that personalising an agent erodes its refusals: compared with a base agent that does not evolve from user feedback, \"the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0--39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning\" against indirect prompt injection.",

"Caveats: all five papers are preprints and none is peer reviewed. The Scale AI paper names its four configurations only in the results section, not the abstract, and all six of its authors are listed as Scale AI. The skills study measures what skill text says, not what agents did, and reports no incidents arising from the directives. The poisoning work used Qwen3 research models pretrained from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B, not production systems. Anthropic says the agent's leans were deliberately strengthened so real-world effects may be smaller, and that its no-agent comparison group differed in experience, so that comparison is not causal."

lines: { "name": "TokenPost", "url": "https://www.tokenpost.com/news/technology/45622" }
"bullets": [

-        "The Decoder, citing a customer email from Anthropic, reported on 31 October that the company is extending its text watermark to Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with Claude Opus 5.5 already carrying it. Anthropic describes the mark as an \"imperceptible pattern in word choice\" that adds no extra characters or tokens, does not change pricing or request and response formats, and \"contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude\". Because it is embedded at the model level, customers cannot switch it off.",

+        "The Decoder, citing a customer email from Anthropic, reported on 31 October that the company is extending its text watermark to Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with Claude Opus 5.5 already carrying it. Anthropic describes the mark as an \"imperceptible pattern in word choice\" that adds no extra characters or tokens, does not change pricing or request and response formats, and \"contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude\". The Decoder says customers cannot turn it off, and that \"Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now.\"",

"On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the watermark applies only while temperature, top_p and top_k stay at their defaults, so changing any one of them avoids the mark; Anthropic's email tells developers who rely on the watermark for compliance to \"keep these settings at their defaults\". The Decoder says that caveat does not appear for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, and that models released after 2 August 2026 shipped with the watermark from day one.",

"xAI said in an announcement on X, reported on 31 October, that invisible statistical watermarking becomes the default for Grok API text output on 7 November 2026 across grok-4.7, grok-4.6, grok-4.5, grok-4.3 and grok-4.20, covering api.x.ai, the Responses API and the Chat Completions API. Crypto Briefing says xAI states the watermark \"does not change the length, quality, or speed of responses\". Team administrators can turn it off per model in the xAI Console, but both outlets say that is limited to specific legal exceptions and compliance needs rather than a general opt-out.",

"Caveats: Anthropic has published no page on the change, so the account rests on the email The Decoder quotes, and The Decoder ties the staged rollout to the EU AI Act's December deadline rather than quoting Anthropic on the reason. xAI's own news index carried no post on this during the week, so the Grok details come from two reports of the same X announcement. Neither company has published a detector or said how the mark can be checked by a third party. Consumer-facing Grok products are not affected, both outlets say."

lines: "The Decoder, citing a customer email from Anthropic, reported on 31 October that the company is extending its text watermark to Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with Claude Opus 5.5 already carrying it. Anthropic describes the mark as an \"imperceptible pattern in word choice\" that adds no extra characters or tokens, does not change pricing or request and response formats, and \"contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude\". The Decoder says customers cannot turn it off, and that \"Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now.\"",

"On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the watermark applies only while temperature, top_p and top_k stay at their defaults, so changing any one of them avoids the mark; Anthropic's email tells developers who rely on the watermark for compliance to \"keep these settings at their defaults\". The Decoder says that caveat does not appear for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, and that models released after 2 August 2026 shipped with the watermark from day one.",

"xAI said in an announcement on X, reported on 31 October, that invisible statistical watermarking becomes the default for Grok API text output on 7 November 2026 across grok-4.7, grok-4.6, grok-4.5, grok-4.3 and grok-4.20, covering api.x.ai, the Responses API and the Chat Completions API. Crypto Briefing says xAI states the watermark \"does not change the length, quality, or speed of responses\". Team administrators can turn it off per model in the xAI Console, but both outlets say that is limited to specific legal exceptions and compliance needs rather than a general opt-out.",

"Three disclosure regimes moved in opposite directions in the same week. HHS published a final rule on 28 October removing the model-card requirements it describes as documents that \"essentially function as nutrition labels\", recording that \"A large majority of commenters were not supportive of our proposal\". Anthropic and xAI both switched on invisible text watermarking, reported on 31 October; The Decoder writes that \"Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now.\" New York's law, signed 28 October and recorded as \"signed chap.368\", requires an AI companion to stop pretending to be a real person to a minor and to verify age.",

"The same mechanism — telling a user what a system is and what it was built from — is being written into law in two jurisdictions and out of certification in a third. The documents do not refer to one another: the HHS rule's stated grounds concern certified health IT; Anthropic's stated reason, per The Decoder, is the EU deadline; and New York's law addresses AI companions and minors. What they share is the obligation, the week, and in two of the three cases a European deadline the American rule does not mention.",

-        "Two of the three obligations carry a gap the sources name themselves. On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the watermark applies only while temperature, top_p and top_k stay at their defaults, and Anthropic's email tells developers relying on it for compliance to \"keep these settings at their defaults\". HHS's stated ground for removal, in full, is that it \"identified no evidence through peer reviewed publication or trade press indicating that users of certified health IT have relied on the transparency requirements or that the requirements have positively impacted patient care\"."

"As of 2 November, the Monday before the midterm elections, Congress has still not voted on a frontier-AI measure and the binding instruments of the week are a state law and a federal deregulatory rule. Nextgov reports three technology bills introduced in the House on 29 October, two of them going to AI infrastructure and congressional capacity: one requiring data centre operators to report to the Energy Information Administration on ownership, expected energy and water usage, whether they have signed non-disclosure agreements with government officials, and whether facilities sit \"within 1,000 feet of a school, national park, hospital, or home\", with failures to disclose \"subjected to fines of as much as $1 million per day\"; one establishing an independent Congressional Office of Technology, reviving the Office of Technology Assessment \"which operated from 1974 to 1995\". Neither has had a committee vote.",

"The state instrument is New York's. Governor Hochul signed S.9051B/A.10379C on 28 October, the Senate record shows it \"signed chap.368\", and the bill text states \"this act shall take effect January 1, 2027\". For users under 18, and any user a company has not confirmed is not a minor, it bars an AI companion from \"pretending to be a real person, to be alive or to have human emotions\", from \"claiming a personal, romantic, professional or authority-figure relationship with a child\" and from \"encouraging kids to keep secrets, isolate themselves or avoid asking parents, trusted adults or professionals for help\". The attorney general may seek \"civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation\" plus \"damages, restitution, the destruction of unlawfully collected data or any AI models trained on it\". In the capability tests, Epoch AI and Irregular both measured Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3, and Reuters reports NIST described it as the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date.",

"Treasury's proposed rule, published on 26 October, is written about the same country and the same category of software, and its stated reason for dropping the compute threshold is that \"no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models\". Its proposed definition covers \"a harness for agentic capability\" — the kind of software the threat-intelligence reports describe operators using. The rule does not mention GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi or any of the vendor reports.",

-        "Nothing in the record links them causally and no source this week attempted to. The threat-intelligence vendors say they do not attribute their campaigns to a named state actor: Dream writes \"we do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor\", and CrowdStrike states that \"This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation.\" Epoch says it triggered no refusals from any provider, including Z.ai, and Reuters reports Z.ai \"did not immediately respond to a request for comment\"."

+        "What the vendors attribute, they attribute to themselves, and no government has attributed any of these campaigns. CrowdStrike names VAPOR PANDA and describes the campaign as China-nexus; Microsoft names Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet among North Korean threat actors; Dream writes \"we do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor\" while saying \"multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation\"; and CrowdStrike states that \"This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation.\" None of them links a model's provenance to a state's involvement, and no source this week connected the capability tests to the intrusions. Epoch says it triggered no refusals from any provider, including Z.ai, and Reuters reports Z.ai \"did not immediately respond to a request for comment\"."

"The tools were targets as well. Cursor shut its extension marketplace after two tampered Claude Code builds planted SSH backdoors, and Wiz counted at least nine AI developer platforms disclosing incidents in October. Anthropic filed to list on Nasdaq as ANT on first-half revenue of $16,286 million, with $131.7 billion of cash and about $417 billion of committed compute payments; four days later Blackstone told investors to expect a double B range rating. Alphabet reported free cash flow of negative $9,065 million, Amazon an outflow of $42.4 billion, and tech stocks lost more than $1 trillion on Friday.",
    "Epoch AI said the open-weight GLM 5.3 built working Firefox exploits at roughly $1,000 each, and Reuters reported NIST calling it the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date. HHS finalised the removal of AI model-card requirements from health IT certification against a large majority of comments; New York's AI companion law for minors became Chapter 368; and the UN First Committee voted 163 to 5, with 9 abstentions, toward autonomous-weapons negotiations. Both OpenAI and Anthropic posted model-generated refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis hours apart, with the appendix of Anthropic's paper stating that \"at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it\"."

Canada's Cyber Centre published a threat bulletin saying that Storm-0940 used an agentic AI framework known as ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and that the actor moved from selecting a target to gaining privileged access to cloud systems in less than three hours. Every one of those is CrowdStrike's own telemetry, and no government has attributed the campaign." },

{ "text": "Now set that against the other half of the record, because I don't think these two agree. On the buyers' side of the same trade, Alphabet reported free cash flow of negative $9,065 million. Amazon reported an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months while holding capital expenditure guidance at approximately $220 billion. Reuters found the biggest spenders returned 9.3 per cent of their operating cash to shareholders, down from 27.4 per cent a year earlier. On Friday, tech stocks erased more than $1 trillion in value." },

{ "text": "And then the mathematics, which is the oddest item of the week. Scientific American reports that mere hours after OpenAI's announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving the same hypothesis, with Claude, Anthropic listed as the author. Anthropic's appendix says the Lean development was written by AI models and reviewed by other instances of the same models, and that at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it. The people who proposed the hypothesis are now examining the OpenAI result, and OpenAI is sponsoring the conference about it." }

    Three renderings of one quotation, attributed to two different speakers across the file.

    The record's 5,000 is Cursor's count of affected users, not machines, and the same unknown's evidence_ends concedes no machine count exists.

    Label misattributes the figure (it is quoted from Cursor's own notice in the record) and asserts an absence the file elsewhere contradicts.

    The item cites an edition outside the stated period, and its bullets[3] event (TechCrunch, 1 November) is only in that 2 November edition.
